n: Dated March 585 BC—after Jerusalem had fallen—this is a funeral lament for Pharaoh.

f.w: in the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, in the first day
f.g: About March 585 BC.

n: Pharaoh saw himself as a young lion among nations, but he is really a sea monster thrashing in the Nile, churning and muddying the waters—causing chaos rather than order.

f.w: a young lion of the nations
a whale
f.g: Hebrew tannin—a sea monster or crocodile, as in 29:3.

n: God will throw his net over Pharaoh using many peoples and haul him out.

f.w: I will therefore spread out my net over thee

n: He will be flung onto dry land as food for birds and beasts.

f.w: I will cast thee forth upon the open field

n: His enormous carcass will cover mountains and fill valleys—exaggerated imagery of total defeat.

f.w: thy height
f.g: Possibly “your rotting remains”—the Hebrew is uncertain.

n: His blood will soak the land up to the mountains and fill the streams.

f.w: the rivers shall be full of thee
f.g: Recalls the Nile turned to blood in Moses’ day.

n: When his light is snuffed out, God will darken the sky—sun, moon, and stars. Cosmic darkness is a recurring image for the day of the Lord.

f.w: I will cover the sun with a cloud

n: All the bright lights of heaven will go dark over Egypt—fitting for a land that worshipped the sun god Ra.

f.w: set darkness upon thy land

n: Many peoples will be troubled when news of Egypt’s fall spreads to distant lands.

f.w: vex the hearts
f.g: Trouble, disturb.

n: Kings will shudder and tremble for their own lives when God brandishes his sword.

f.w: they shall tremble at every moment

n: Plainly stated: Babylon’s sword is coming against Egypt.

f.w: The sword of the king of Babylon

n: Egypt’s pride and its crowds will be crushed by the most ruthless of nations.

f.w: the pomp of Egypt
f.g: Egypt’s pride and splendor.

n: Even its cattle will be gone, so no foot or hoof will muddy the waters anymore.

f.w: neither shall the foot of man trouble them

n: With nothing stirring them, the waters will settle and flow smoothly like oil—an eerie calm over an empty land.

f.w: cause their rivers to run like oil
f.g: Still, clear, and slow-moving.

n: When Egypt is emptied and struck, they will know the Lord.

f.w: destitute of that whereof it was full
f.g: Stripped of its abundance.

n: This lament will be chanted by the women of the nations, as professional mourners did at funerals.

f.w: the daughters of the nations shall lament her

n: Two weeks later (in the same year) comes a final oracle: a vision of Egypt descending to the realm of the dead.

f.w: in the fifteenth day of the month
f.g: Probably of the twelfth month, two weeks after v. 1.

n: Ezekiel is to wail for Egypt and, by his prophetic word, send her down to the underworld with other great nations.

f.w: cast them down
f.g: The prophet’s word accomplishes what it announces.

n: “Are you more beautiful than anyone? Go down and lie with the uncircumcised!” Egypt’s pride counts for nothing in death.

f.w: Whom dost thou pass in beauty?

n: Egypt will fall among those killed by the sword and be dragged away with her multitudes.

f.w: draw her
f.g: Drag her off.

n: The mighty dead in Sheol will greet Pharaoh and his allies: “They have come down; they lie with the uncircumcised.”

f.w: out of the midst of hell
f.g: From Sheol, the realm of the dead.

n: Assyria is there, surrounded by the graves of her soldiers, all killed by the sword.

f.w: Asshur
f.g: Assyria, the empire that fell in 612–609 BC.

n: Her graves lie in the deepest part of the pit. She once spread terror among the living; now she lies with the slain.

f.w: the sides of the pit
f.g: The farthest depths of the underworld.

n: Elam (in western Iran) is there too, once terrifying, now bearing shame with the dead.

f.w: Elam
f.g: An ancient kingdom east of Babylon, conquered by Assyria.

n: Elam lies on a bed among the slain, her shame now complete.

f.w: They have set her a bed
f.g: Her place in the grave.

n: Meshech and Tubal, warlike peoples of Asia Minor, are there as well.

f.w: Meshech, Tubal
f.g: Peoples of Anatolia; they reappear in chapters 38–39 with Gog.

n: They do not receive the honorable burial of ancient heroes, who were buried with weapons under their heads. Their sins rest on their bones.

f.w: they have laid their swords under their heads
f.g: Honored warriors were buried with their weapons.

f.w: the mighty that are fallen

n: Pharaoh, you too will be broken and lie among the uncircumcised and the slain.

f.w: thou shalt be broken

n: Edom, its kings, and princes lie there, despite all their might.

f.w: There is Edom

n: So do the princes of the north and the Sidonians—ashamed of the power that once caused terror.

f.w: the princes of the north
f.g: Probably Phoenician and Syrian rulers.

f.w: Zidonians

n: Pharaoh will see them and find grim “comfort” that he is not alone in his fall.

f.w: shall be comforted
f.g: Consoled in a bitter sense—misery has company.

n: God allowed Pharaoh to spread terror in the land of the living, but in the end he will lie among the slain. Earthly power always ends, but God’s purposes do not. The oracles against the nations end here.

f.w: I have caused my terror in the land of the living
f.g: Some manuscripts read “his terror.”
